description: Hand-written source for the Engineering Encyclopedia: concept entries that the catalogue does not hold (definitions, synonyms, abbreviations, shop terms, relations between concepts) and the calculators each concept is calculated with. Calculator identities, names, labs, categories, tiers and aliases come from catalog/gearhead-catalog.json and the engine, never from here. catalog/build-encyclopedia.js joins the two into catalog/gearhead-encyclopedia.json; catalog/check-encyclopedia.js validates both.

provenance_default.note: Definitions in this file were drafted for the Issue #23 proof of concept (2026-10-26). They have NOT been reviewed by the owner or checked against a cited source: review.status is draft-unreviewed and sources is empty until someone reviews them. Do not change a status to reviewed without a named reviewer and date.

relation_types.broader: the target is the more general concept (this entry is a kind or part of it)
relation_types.narrower: the target is a more specific concept
relation_types.prerequisite: the target must be known or calculated first
relation_types.not-equivalent: often confused with this entry but NOT the same quantity; a note saying why is required

ambiguous.note: Shop shorthand for a compression ratio. It usually means the static (mechanical) ratio, but the dynamic and crankcase ratios are different quantities.
Without a qualifier it usually means the static ratio; the dynamic ratio (from the intake valve closing point) and a two-stroke crankcase ratio are different quantities.
Used for a suspension spring and for a valve spring; the calculators are different.

concepts.definition: The ratio of the cylinder volume with the piston at bottom dead centre to the volume with it at top dead centre, from the full swept volume plus the clearance volume (chamber, gasket, deck and piston dome or dish).
concepts.distinctions: It is fixed by geometry. It is not the pressure measured on a compression gauge, and it is not the dynamic ratio, which starts compression only when the intake valve closes.

related.note: The dynamic ratio uses only the stroke left after the intake valve closes, so it is always lower.
Cranking compression is a measured pressure (psi or bar), not a volume ratio.

concepts.definition: The compression ratio counted from the moment the intake valve closes, using the piston position at intake valve closing instead of bottom dead centre.
concepts.distinctions: It depends on the camshaft (intake valve closing point) and rod length as well as the static geometry.

related.note: The static ratio uses the full stroke; the dynamic ratio only the part after the intake valve closes.

concepts.definition: In a crankcase-scavenged two-stroke engine, the ratio of the crankcase volume with the piston at top dead centre to the volume with it at bottom dead centre.
concepts.distinctions: It describes the crankcase pumping that transfers the charge, not compression in the combustion chamber.

related.note: Measured in the crankcase of a two-stroke, not in the cylinder.

concepts.definition: The crankshaft angle, usually given in degrees after bottom dead centre, at which the intake valve closes.
concepts.distinctions: Cam cards give it at a stated lift (advertised or 0.050 in); figures at different lift references are not interchangeable.

concepts.definition: The total volume swept by all the pistons in one stroke: bore area times stroke times the number of cylinders.
concepts.distinctions: It excludes the clearance (combustion chamber) volume.

concepts.definition: Cylinder bore divided by piston stroke. Above 1 the engine is called oversquare, below 1 undersquare.

related.note: The rod/stroke ratio compares the connecting rod length, not the bore, with the stroke.

concepts.definition: Connecting rod centre-to-centre length divided by the crankshaft stroke.
concepts.distinctions: It sets the connecting rod angle and how the piston moves near top and bottom dead centre.

related.note: Compares rod length, not bore, with the stroke.

concepts.definition: The average speed of the piston over a crank revolution: twice the stroke times the engine speed.

The constant pressure that, acting on the pistons over each power stroke, would give the engine's measured brake (output) torque. It compares torque per unit displacement between engines of different sizes.

related.note: IMEP is the indicated (in-cylinder) value; BMEP is what remains at the crankshaft.

concepts.definition: The mean effective pressure from the work done by the gas on the pistons, before friction and pumping losses.

related.note: BMEP is IMEP minus the friction and pumping losses (FMEP).

concepts.definition: The part of the indicated mean effective pressure lost to engine friction (and, in many definitions, pumping): IMEP minus BMEP.
The cylinder pressure read on a compression gauge while the engine is turned by the starter.
concepts.distinctions: It is a measured pressure that depends on cranking speed, valve timing and sealing, not a geometric ratio.

concepts.definition: The gap between the two ends of a piston ring when it is installed square in the cylinder bore.
The last gear reduction between the transmission output and the driven wheels, normally the differential's ring-and-pinion ratio.
concepts.distinctions: The overall ratio in a given gear is the transmission gear ratio times the final drive ratio (times any transfer case or drop-box ratio).

concepts.definition: The pair of gears in a differential: the pinion on the driveshaft input turns the ring gear on the differential carrier. Their tooth-count ratio is the axle ratio.
The ratio of input-shaft to output-shaft speed of the transmission in a given gear.
A sun gear, planet gears on a carrier and an outer ring gear. Holding or driving different members gives different ratios; automatic transmissions are built from them.
The engine speed reached with the converter output held stationary at full throttle, set by the converter design and the engine torque.
concepts.distinctions: Flash stall (on a launch) and brake stall (against the brakes) are measured differently and differ.

concepts.definition: A differential that limits the speed difference between the two driven wheels so torque can still reach the wheel with more grip.
concepts.distinctions: A locker is a different device (it locks the axles together); shop talk often lumps them together.

concepts.definition: For a limited-slip differential, the largest ratio of torque between the high-traction and low-traction wheels that it can sustain before the wheels slip relative to each other.

The angle between the two shafts joined by a universal joint. A single U-joint running at an angle makes the output speed fluctuate twice per revolution; equal and opposite angles at the two ends of a driveshaft cancel it.
The rotational speed at which a driveshaft's first bending natural frequency is excited, so it whirls and can fail.
The most torque a clutch can transmit without slipping, set by clamp load, friction coefficient, mean friction radius and the number of friction surfaces.
The force needed to compress a suspension spring by a unit distance, measured at the spring.
concepts.distinctions: It is not the wheel rate: the rate felt at the wheel is reduced by the motion ratio squared.

related.note: Wheel rate = spring rate × motion ratio².

concepts.definition: The force needed to compress a valve spring by a unit distance, used with installed height and lift to find seat and open pressures.
The ratio of spring or damper travel to wheel travel for a given suspension movement.
concepts.distinctions: Some sources define it the other way up (wheel travel over spring travel); check which convention a calculator uses.

concepts.definition: The effective spring rate measured at the wheel: the spring rate multiplied by the square of the motion ratio (spring travel over wheel travel).
The natural frequency at which a corner of the sprung mass bounces on its wheel rate, usually given in hertz or cycles per minute.
The point, in a front or rear view, about which the sprung mass rolls relative to the ground under a lateral force, found from the suspension link geometry.
The moment needed to roll the body by one degree (or radian), from the springs and anti-roll bars of an axle.
concepts.distinctions: The front-to-rear split of roll stiffness (roll couple distribution) is a separate quantity from either axle's roll stiffness.

concepts.definition: The share of the rear weight transfer under acceleration that the suspension geometry carries through the links instead of the springs, given as a percentage.
The share of the front weight transfer under braking that the suspension geometry carries through the links instead of the springs, given as a percentage.
The change in vertical tyre load between front and rear (under acceleration or braking) or between left and right (in a corner), caused by the centre of gravity being above the ground.
concepts.distinctions: It is load moving between tyres; the vehicle's total weight does not change.

concepts.definition: The angle of the wheels relative to the vehicle centreline seen from above: toe-in when the fronts of the tyres point towards each other, toe-out when they point apart.
The change of toe as the suspension moves up and down, from the steering linkage not following the suspension arcs.
The fore-and-aft tilt of the steering axis seen from the side; positive caster tilts the top of the axis rearward.
The inward or outward tilt of the wheel seen from the front; negative camber tilts the top of the wheel inward.
Steering geometry in which the inside front wheel turns more than the outside so both follow circles about a common centre.
